/FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Issued at 230 AM CST Thu Nov 12 2026

Cool and Dry Continues Friday:

Temperatures and dew points continue falling on Friday. Local
climatology indicates that the median high at Vichy-Rolla with 
an 850mb temperature of -7C and clear/partly cloudy skies is 41
degrees, and 34 degrees under mostly cloudy/overcast skies.
Skies are currently expected to be mostly cloudy towards central
Missouri, so it may be quite the brisk day for portions of our
area on Friday. Cloud cover will decrease with southern and
western extent, allowing for warmer temperatures. As cloud cover
extent becomes further refined on Friday, temperatures will as
well. Cloudier portions of central Missouri are likely to only 
reach low 40s, while areas with more sunshine will reach upper
40s to near 50 degrees. Dew points in the low 20s will make it
feel quite dry, with afternoon RHs as low as 30%-35%. 


Synoptic Evolution:

The ridging aloft shifts over the central US on Saturday,
with troughing over the West squeezing the ridge between it and
the trough over the East Coast. A southern stream shortwave 
pushes into Southern California on Friday and into the southern 
Plains by Sunday, quickly becoming cut off Sunday into Monday as
it loses upper jet support. Ensembles start to diverge on the
evolution of the synoptic pattern around this time as numerous
shortwaves across the country become less clearly resolved, but
trends over the last 24 hours have seen PoPs come in lower and 
slower for Sunday and Monday. The Euro is currently favoring a 
solution where the low becomes closed earlier and further west,
bringing less energy into the area overall and keeping PoPs
confined to areas further west and south. After the wave is
absorbed, all ensembles point to a broadening of the ridging in
place over most of the CONUS.


Temperatures Saturday and Beyond:

The height rises associated with the ridging over the central
CONUS will allow temperatures to gradually rise on Saturday
onward. Some uncertainty in Sunday's temperatures does result
from questions about precipitation and cloud cover associated
with the disturbance to our south, but a general warming trend
emerges by next week. Weekend temperatures in the low 50s rise
into the low 60s by Thursday, becoming more seasonable for mid-
November. 


Precip Chances Sunday/Monday:

As the disturbance pushes south of us on Sunday and Monday, PoPs
begin to increase to 15-25% in our far southwest counties 
during the day on Sunday, which as high as the NBM brings them
for this system. The LREF is more generous, keeping the NBM's
prior 10-45% chances across the western half of our area. Overall
QPF amounts are currently 0 for most of the area, peaking 
around 0.06" in McDonald County with measurable precip not even 
extending as far east as Springfield or as far north as Nevada.
So, even if it does precipitate, it won't be very much, if at
all. Most of the area will likely stay dry Sunday into Monday,
especially areas east of Highway 65 and north of Highway 60. 

As far as precip type goes............ this will depend heavily
on timing and duration of any rainfall. With highs on Sunday in
the upper 40s to low 50s, precipitation will begin as rain, 
there's no question about that, especially since the highest 
PoPs are during the afternoon hours. Global ensembles, including
the most conservative Euro ensemble, do keep low PoPs lingering
through Sunday night. If rain continues into Sunday night as 
temperatures begin to drop, it becomes more likely that the 10% 
PoPs would turn from rain PoPs to flurry PoPs. But the other 
factor to consider is that GFS model soundings currently show 
10,000 feet of dry air in the lowest level that precipitation of
any type will have to overcome before it ever reaches the 
ground. Many variables to monitor in the coming days, but
regardless of if these areas receive <0.1" of rain or a few 
flakes that melt as soon as they hit the ground, no impacts are
expected from either outcome.
